candidates.quote: Wherefore he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order the heaven, he made this image eternal but moving according to number, while eternity itself rests in unity; and this image we call time.
candidates.author: Plato
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives the month its founding idea: what passes is not the opposite of what stays but its likeness in motion.

candidates.quote: Some races wax and others wane, and in a short space the tribes of living things are changed, and like runners hand on the torch of life.
candidates.author: Lucretius
candidates.locator: Book II, lines 77 to 79 (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1910)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Passing on is made an action rather than a loss, which is the kindest thing impermanence can be told at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.
candidates.author: Augustine of Hippo
candidates.locator: Book XI, chapter 14 (trans. E. B. Pusey, 1838)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A reader waking into an ordinary morning is told that the thing carrying them away has never been explained by anyone, which is company rather than alarm.

candidates.quote: Firewood becomes ash, and it does not become firewood again.
candidates.author: Dōgen
candidates.whyThisMonth: The plainest statement of impermanence in the tradition that thought hardest about it, and it is about a wood stove, not a deathbed.

candidates.quote: Life is a pure flame, and we live by an invisible sun within us.
candidates.author: Thomas Browne
candidates.whyThisMonth: One of the great sentences in English prose, and it answers the month's question by pointing at what burns rather than at what is spent.

candidates.quote: A free man thinks of death least of all things; and his wisdom is a meditation not of death but of life.
candidates.author: Baruch Spinoza
candidates.locator: Part IV, Proposition 67 (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The one line that keeps an elegiac month from tipping over: it turns the whole subject toward living without denying the subject.

candidates.quote: If by eternity is understood not endless temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present.
candidates.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
candidates.whyThisMonth: It hands the reader the one form of permanence that a passing morning can actually contain.

candidates.quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.
candidates.author: Henri Bergson
candidates.whyThisMonth: Impermanence described as accumulation rather than subtraction: nothing is being taken away, the whole of it is arriving.

candidates.quote: Life is not a series of gig lamps symmetrically arranged; but a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope surrounding us from the beginning of consciousness to the end.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the essay is known by, and it says the day will not arrive in tidy separate lamps, which is a useful thing to be told before it starts.

candidates.quote: Attachment is a manufacturer of illusions and whoever wants reality ought to be detached.
candidates.author: Simone Weil
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month's hard counsel, put as a claim about seeing clearly rather than as a demand to feel less.

candidates.quote: The remedy for unpredictability, for the chaotic uncertainty of the future, is contained in the faculty to make and keep promises.
candidates.author: Hannah Arendt
candidates.locator: chapter V, section 33 (University of Chicago Press, 1958)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month's second half in one sentence: against a future that will not hold still, a kept promise is the thing that stays.

candidates.quote: For nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed; the earth is always shifting, the light is always changing, the sea does not cease to grind down rock.
candidates.author: James Baldwin
candidates.whyThisMonth: Impermanence stated as a ground to stand on, in a cadence a reader can carry out of the room.

candidates.quote: The answer must be, I think, that beauty and grace are performed whether or not we will or sense them. The least we can do is try to be there.
candidates.author: Annie Dillard
candidates.locator: chapter 1, Heaven and Earth in Jest
candidates.whyThisMonth: If the beautiful thing is going to pass whether or not anyone watches, the only instruction left is to be awake for it, which is the point of the hour.

candidates.quote: All photographs are memento mori. To take a photograph is to participate in another person’s (or thing’s) mortality, vulnerability, mutability.
candidates.author: Susan Sontag
candidates.locator: In Plato’s Cave (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1977)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It catches the month in the most ordinary modern act, so the theme arrives through a phone camera rather than through an urn.

candidates.quote: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
candidates.author: Joan Didion
candidates.work: On Keeping a Notebook, Slouching Towards Bethlehem
candidates.whyThisMonth: The self is the thing that passes fastest, and this asks the reader to stay on speaking terms with the ones already gone.

candidates.quote: But that was the best time of my life, and only now that it has gone from me forever—only now do I realize it.
candidates.author: Natalia Ginzburg
candidates.work: Winter in the Abruzzi, The Little Virtues
candidates.whyThisMonth: The exact ache the month is named for, and it arrives early enough in the day to be spent noticing what is still here.
